subject: biology

items.q: What evidence indicates that an ecosystem has persisted, and so shown stability, for millions of years?
items.correct: Fossil pollen from dated layers of sediment shows the same type of plant community persisting through geological time.
items.misconception: The oldest individual trees now growing in the ecosystem have been dated at several thousand years old.
items.why: Old trees are visible and impressive, and 'ancient forest' is used in everyday speech for a forest with old trees, so students take the age of individuals as the age of the ecosystem. Even the oldest individual trees live for a few thousand years, whereas ecosystem continuity is measured over millions of years. Evidence comes from dated fossil pollen, leaves, wood and animals in sediment layers that show the same type of community present throughout.
items.specStatementText: Ecosystems can stay the same kind of place for millions of years
items.random_wrong: Census data show that the population size of every species has stayed exactly constant from year to year.

items.q: Sediment cores from a desert basin contain pollen in every layer. The layers have been dated to span the last 30 million years, and the deepest layers contain pollen of the same drought-adapted plant families as the surface layers. What is the best conclusion from this evidence?
items.correct: A desert ecosystem has persisted in this region for tens of millions of years, so it has shown long-term stability.
items.misconception: The region cannot have supported a stable ecosystem for so long, because a desert is too harsh to persist for millions of years.
items.why: Students associate stability with abundance and productivity, and deserts are described as 'harsh' and 'extreme', which suggests fragility rather than persistence. Stability is about continuity over time, not about productivity or species richness. The guide allows forest, desert or other ecosystems to illustrate stability, and desert ecosystems provide some of the strongest evidence of persistence over millions of years.
items.specStatementText: Ecosystems can stay the same kind of place for millions of years
items.random_wrong: The plants whose pollen is in the deepest layers must still be alive today for the ecosystem to count as stable.

items.q: Which set of conditions is required for an ecosystem to remain stable?
items.correct: A continuing supply of energy, recycling of nutrients, genetic diversity and climatic variables staying within tolerance levels.
items.misconception: Recycling of both energy and nutrients, genetic diversity and climatic variables staying within tolerance levels.
items.why: The word 'cycle' is used for carbon and nitrogen, and diagrams of ecosystems draw arrows from decomposers back to plants, so students assume the same loop carries energy. The requirements for stability include a continuous supply of energy and the recycling of nutrients, and these are different. Energy enters as light, is transferred along food chains and leaves as heat; nutrients are recycled by decomposers.
items.specStatementText: What an ecosystem needs to stay stable
items.random_wrong: A continuing supply of energy, recycling of nutrients, large population sizes and climatic variables staying within tolerance levels.

items.q: A plantation forest consists of a single tree species, all grown from cuttings of one parent tree, so the trees are genetically almost identical. A fungal disease that kills this species arrives. Which statement about the stability of this forest is correct?
items.correct: It is vulnerable to collapse because few or no trees carry alleles that give resistance to the disease.
items.misconception: It is as stable as a natural forest, because stability depends on the number of trees, not on their genetic variation.
items.why: Students learn that small populations are vulnerable to extinction and conflate population size with genetic diversity, and they confuse genetic diversity with species diversity. A large population of near-identical individuals can be destroyed by a single disease or environmental change to which none of them is resistant. Genetic diversity provides the variation on which survival and adaptation depend, so it is listed alongside energy supply, nutrient recycling and climate as a requirement for stability.
items.specStatementText: What an ecosystem needs to stay stable
items.random_wrong: It will remain stable, because the energy in the trees killed by the fungus is recycled to support new tree growth.

items.q: In 1970 the area of a rainforest was 4 000 000 km². By 2020 the area was 3 320 000 km². What is the percentage change in the area of forest?
items.why: Students remember that a percentage needs a 'whole' and reach for the most recent figure as the whole, or they divide the smaller number by the larger without thinking about which is the reference. Percentage change is always expressed relative to the original value. For deforestation, the reference is the original area of forest, so the change is divided by the original area.
items.specStatementText: The Amazon: a possible tipping point

items.q: Which statement correctly explains the link between the area of the Amazon rainforest and the rainfall it receives?
items.correct: Transpiration from a large area of trees adds water vapour to the air, which cools, drives air flows and returns as rain over the forest.
items.misconception: Rain over the forest comes from water evaporated from the Atlantic Ocean, so the area of forest has little effect on the rainfall.
items.why: Water cycle diagrams in earlier courses show evaporation from the sea and rain falling on land, with transpiration either omitted or shown as a minor arrow. Transpiration from a large area of trees generates atmospheric water vapour that produces cooling, air flows and rainfall over the forest. This is why a large area of rainforest is needed to maintain the forest's own climate, and why deforestation may push the system past a tipping point.
items.specStatementText: The Amazon: a possible tipping point
items.random_wrong: Every hectare of forest contributes a fixed share of the rainfall, so rainfall falls in exact proportion to the area of forest that is cleared.

items.q: Different research groups have estimated that the Amazon rainforest could reach a tipping point when 20%, 25% or 40% of its original area has been deforested. About 17% has been cleared so far. What does this range of estimates indicate?
items.correct: The minimum area of forest needed to maintain moisture recycling is uncertain, so the tipping point could be close.
items.misconception: Only one of the estimates can be correct, so nothing can be concluded until the other two have been shown to be wrong.
items.why: Media reports often quote a single figure for a threshold, and school science rarely presents estimates with uncertainty, so students expect a single correct value. The guide explicitly includes uncertainty over the minimum area of rainforest that is sufficient to maintain transpiration-driven rainfall. Different models and assumptions give different estimates; this uncertainty is a reason for caution rather than evidence that the estimates are worthless.
items.specStatementText: The Amazon: a possible tipping point
items.random_wrong: Rainfall must already have fallen by 17%, in proportion to the area cleared, so there is no threshold left to estimate.

items.q: Why is a sealed glass vessel preferable to an open tank for a mesocosm used to investigate ecosystem stability?
items.correct: Matter cannot enter or leave the vessel, but light can still enter and heat can still leave.
items.misconception: It forms a completely closed system, so neither matter nor energy can be exchanged with the surroundings.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'sealed' is 'shut off from everything', and 'closed system' is used loosely in earlier courses without distinguishing matter from energy. The point of a sealed glass vessel is that it is closed to matter but open to energy. Light enters and drives photosynthesis; heat leaves. This lets the investigator test whether the ecosystem can recycle its matter while receiving a continuous supply of energy, mirroring the Earth.
items.specStatementText: Mesocosms as models of stability
items.random_wrong: The lid can be removed briefly each day to replace the oxygen that the organisms inside have used up.

items.q: A class plans to use mesocosms to investigate the effect of light intensity on ecosystem stability. Which design is most likely to succeed and to follow IB experimental guidelines?
items.correct: Sealed glass jars containing pond water, algae, small aquatic invertebrates and sediment, placed at different distances from a lamp for several weeks.
items.misconception: Open terraria containing soil, plants and a small lizard, placed at different distances from a lamp, since a terrestrial model is more realistic.
items.why: Students equate realism with size and with the presence of the animals they picture in an ecosystem, and they do not consider gas exchange, water balance or animal welfare. The guide states that aquatic or microbial ecosystems are likely to be more successful than terrestrial ones, because gas exchange and nutrient cycling are easier to maintain in water and the organisms are small with rapid life cycles. Care and maintenance of mesocosms must follow IB experimental guidelines, which do not permit experiments that cause animals to suffer.
items.specStatementText: Mesocosms as models of stability
items.random_wrong: Open tanks of pond water and algae with an air pump running in each, so that the organisms do not run out of oxygen during the investigation.

items.q: Sea otters make up a tiny fraction of the biomass of a kelp forest. Where otters were hunted to extinction, sea urchins multiplied and grazed the kelp down to bare rock, and the fish, seals and seabirds that depended on the kelp disappeared. What does this show about sea otters?
items.correct: They are a keystone species, because their effect on community structure is far greater than their abundance suggests.
items.misconception: They cannot be a keystone species, because a keystone species is one contributing most of the community's biomass.
items.why: The word 'key' suggests 'main' or 'biggest', and in food webs the largest boxes are the abundant producers, so students assume importance follows abundance. The defining feature of a keystone species is a disproportionate impact: a small number of individuals, such as sea otters in a kelp forest, hold the structure of the whole community in place. Removing them risks ecosystem collapse even though they are a tiny fraction of the biomass.
items.specStatementText: Keystone species hold the community together
items.random_wrong: Their removal should only have affected the urchins they ate, so the loss of fish and seabirds must have had a different cause.

items.q: A stock of Atlantic cod has a biomass of 200 000 tonnes. Each year, growth of the fish and recruitment of young fish add 15% to the biomass, while natural mortality removes 5% of it. What is the annual rate of replacement of the stock, below which the catch must stay for harvesting to be sustainable? The rate of replacement is the net change in biomass from these processes.
items.correct: 20 000 tonnes
items.misconception: 10 000 tonnes
items.why: The idea that predators 'only take the weak' is extended to human harvesting, and it is comforting to believe that fishing merely replaces natural deaths. Natural mortality continues whether or not harvesting takes place. The sustainable catch is limited to the net replacement (additions minus natural losses); treating natural deaths as available for harvest overestimates the sustainable catch.
items.specStatementText: Is the harvest sustainable?
items.random_wrong: 30 000 tonnes

items.q: Records for a cod fishery show that the annual catch stayed close to 250 000 tonnes for 20 years. Over the same period the number of fishing days needed to land that catch doubled, and the mean age of the cod caught fell from 8 years to 4 years. What do these data indicate?
items.correct: The stock is being harvested unsustainably: more effort is needed for the same catch and few fish now survive to old age.
items.misconception: Harvesting is sustainable, because the catch has remained constant for two decades and so the stock must be replacing itself.
items.why: The catch is the figure that is recorded and reported, and students assume that a resource in trouble would show it directly in the yield. Assessing sustainability requires comparing harvest rate with replacement rate. Indicators include rising effort for the same catch, falling catch per unit effort, and a fall in the mean age or size of individuals harvested, all of which can occur while the total catch is unchanged.
items.specStatementText: Is the harvest sustainable?
items.random_wrong: Harvesting is sustainable, because cod are a renewable resource that reproduce each year and so cannot be depleted by fishing.

items.q: Which practice increases the sustainability of agriculture on a farm?
items.correct: Growing cover crops between harvests so that the soil is protected from erosion and less nitrate is leached away.
items.misconception: Applying extra inorganic fertilizer every year so that all the nutrients lost by leaching are replaced.
items.why: Fertilizer is introduced as 'the solution' to nutrient loss, and students see only the benefit to crop yield, not the costs of producing and losing it. Sustainability of agriculture requires considering the supply of fertilizers and other inputs, pollution due to agrochemicals, leaching of nutrients and carbon footprint together. Fertilizer applied beyond what the crop can take up is leached away, pollutes water and wastes the energy used to make it.
items.specStatementText: What makes farming unsustainable
items.random_wrong: Ploughing sloping fields deeply each year, because soil is replaced by weathering as fast as it is lost.

items.q: Nitrate and phosphate leached from farmland enter a lake. Which sequence of events leads to the death of fish in the lake?
items.correct: Algal bloom → algae die → aerobic bacteria decompose them → dissolved oxygen falls → fish suffocate
items.misconception: Fertilizer enters the lake → fish absorb nitrate across their gills → it poisons them → fish die
items.why: Fertilizers are chemicals, chemicals in water are assumed to be poisons, and the chain of events through algae and bacteria is long and indirect. Eutrophication kills fish indirectly. Nitrate and phosphate stimulate an algal bloom; when the algae die, aerobic saprotrophic bacteria decompose them, raising biochemical oxygen demand and depleting dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate.
items.specStatementText: Eutrophication and biochemical oxygen demand
items.random_wrong: Algal bloom → algae die → BOD falls as the algae decay → less oxygen dissolves in the water → fish suffocate

items.q: Water was sampled at three points on a river: A, upstream of a farm; B, 2 km downstream of the farm's drainage outlet; and C, 15 km downstream. Nitrate concentration (mg dm⁻³) was 1 at A, 12 at B and 3 at C. BOD (mg dm⁻³) was 2 at A, 14 at B and 4 at C. The number of fish species found was 8 at A, 1 at B and 6 at C. Which explanation fits these data?
items.correct: Nitrate at B caused an algal bloom whose decomposition raised BOD and removed oxygen, so fish were lost.
items.misconception: Algae stimulated by the nitrate at B released extra oxygen by photosynthesis, so the fish must have been lost for another reason.
items.why: Students learn that plants and algae produce oxygen and apply this logically to a bloom without considering what happens when the algae die. The effect of eutrophication that matters is increased biochemical oxygen demand. The mass of dead algae is decomposed by aerobic bacteria whose respiration depletes dissolved oxygen, so eutrophic water becomes hypoxic and fish and invertebrates die.
items.specStatementText: Eutrophication and biochemical oxygen demand
items.random_wrong: The BOD of 14 at B shows that the water there holds the most oxygen, so lack of oxygen cannot explain the loss of fish there.

items.q: In a study of an estuary, DDT concentrations were measured in parts per million (ppm): water 0.00005, plankton 0.04, small fish 0.5, larger predatory fish 2, fish-eating birds 25. Which statement explains this pattern?
items.correct: DDT is fat-soluble and not excreted, so each consumer retains the DDT from all its prey and the concentration rises at each trophic level.
items.misconception: Birds live longer than fish, so the pattern is due only to each bird having had more years in which to accumulate DDT.
items.why: Longevity does contribute, and the two processes have similar names, so students merge them and miss the role of feeding on already-contaminated prey. A consumer takes in the toxin present in every prey organism it eats, and because the toxin is retained, its concentration in the consumer becomes higher than in the prey. This step-up at each trophic level is biomagnification, and it occurs even between organisms of similar age.
items.specStatementText: Biomagnification: DDT and mercury
items.random_wrong: Each organism absorbed DDT directly from the water, so the birds must have been exposed to more contaminated water.

items.q: Why does mercury released from industry reach high concentrations in large predatory fish such as tuna?
items.correct: Mercury taken in with prey is retained in tissues rather than excreted, so its concentration rises at each trophic level up to the tuna.
items.misconception: Large fish swallow the greatest volume of water while feeding, so they take in more mercury than smaller fish do.
items.why: Students confuse the total amount of a substance with its concentration, and assume that a large animal must eat more than the whole of the trophic level below it. Biomagnification concerns concentration. Each trophic level has less biomass than the one below, yet retains the persistent toxin from all the prey eaten, so the toxin becomes concentrated in a smaller mass of tissue.
items.specStatementText: Biomagnification: DDT and mercury
items.random_wrong: Tuna swim through polluted water for years and absorb mercury through their gills rather than from their food.

items.q: Which statement about plastic pollution of the oceans is correct?
items.correct: Macroplastics fragment into microplastics but are not broken down by decomposers, so the material persists.
items.misconception: Marine bacteria biodegrade plastics, but so slowly that the material persists for a few decades before disappearing.
items.why: Students see plastic become brittle and fragment, and assume that physical breakup is the same as biological breakdown. Fragmentation by sunlight and wave action converts macroplastics into microplastics, but the polymer is not decomposed. Plastics are persistent in the environment because of their non-biodegradability, and microplastics remain and enter food chains.
items.specStatementText: Plastics persist, and public understanding drove action
items.random_wrong: Microplastics are too small to harm marine animals, so only macroplastics have effects on marine life.

items.q: Which statement describes the approach used to restore native forest at Hinewai Reserve in New Zealand?
items.correct: Grazing livestock were removed and introduced gorse was left as a nurse canopy, under which native trees regenerated with minimal interference.
items.misconception: Native tree seedlings were raised in nurseries and planted across the whole reserve in place of the former pasture and scrub.
items.why: Tree planting is the most visible form of environmental restoration, and students assume that restoration must be done by people rather than by natural processes. At Hinewai Reserve native forest regenerated without planting, through minimal interference once livestock were removed. Rewilding may involve ecological management, such as controlling introduced species, but its aim is to re-establish the natural processes that then maintain the ecosystem.
items.specStatementText: Rewilding: let natural processes do the work
items.random_wrong: The introduced gorse was cleared with herbicide and machinery before native forest was allowed to return to the area.

items.q: Which of these is a method used in rewilding to restore natural processes in an ecosystem?
items.correct: Re-establishing connectivity between areas of habitat over a large region so that animals can move between them.
items.misconception: Removing apex predators from the area so that the populations of herbivores and other prey species can increase in size.
items.why: Predators are seen as destructive, and the effect of a predator is traced only to its immediate prey rather than through the food web. Reintroduction of apex predators and other keystone species is a rewilding method precisely because of their disproportionate positive effect on community structure. After wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995, changes in elk numbers and grazing were followed by recovery of vegetation and of species that depend on it.
items.specStatementText: Rewilding: let natural processes do the work
items.random_wrong: Replanting the whole area with nursery-grown trees and maintaining it by continuous intensive management.

items.q: Alder trees colonising ground exposed by a retreating glacier have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules. Within decades the soil nitrogen content rises and spruce trees, which cannot grow on the bare ground, replace the alders. Which statement about the cause of this change is correct?
items.correct: It is a biotic cause: the alders changed the soil so that other species could establish and then outcompete them.
items.misconception: It is an abiotic cause, because only changes in the physical environment such as glacial retreat can drive succession.
items.why: The examples used to introduce succession are dramatic physical events, so the physical event is remembered as the cause of the whole process. The guide states that succession can be triggered by changes in both the abiotic environment and biotic factors. Each stage of succession is driven largely by the organisms of the previous stage changing the environment, for example nitrogen-fixing alders enriching soil so that spruce can grow.
items.specStatementText: Succession and what triggers it
items.random_wrong: The alders enriched the soil in order to prepare the site for the spruce trees that follow them in the succession.

items.q: Surveys were made on land exposed by a retreating glacier 10, 50, 100 and 200 years earlier. Mean plant height was 0.1 m, 3 m, 15 m and 30 m; the number of plant species was 6, 18, 25 and 31; and net primary production (kg m⁻² yr⁻¹) was 0.05, 0.4, 0.9 and 1.2. Soil depth and organic content increased throughout. Which conclusion do the data support?
items.correct: Plant size, species diversity and primary production all increased as the primary succession proceeded.
items.misconception: The rise in species number is misleading, because the hardy pioneer community at 10 years was the most diverse stage.
items.why: Students imagine an empty space being colonized by everything that arrives, and picture the later forest as a few large trees. The pioneer community consists of a few species able to tolerate bare ground. As soil forms and plants grow larger, more habitats and food sources exist, so species diversity and food web complexity increase during primary succession.
items.specStatementText: What changes as primary succession proceeds
items.random_wrong: Net primary production should have fallen after 100 years because mature trees grow slowly, so the 200-year value must be wrong.

items.q: On a heather moor, heather plants pass through pioneer, building, mature and degenerate phases. In the degenerate phase the central branches die, opening a gap that is colonised by lichens and mosses before heather seedlings re-establish there. What does this show?
items.correct: The community follows a cycle of phases driven by the heather's own ageing, rather than settling into one unchanging climax.
items.misconception: The moor has not yet reached its climax, which will be a permanent heather community with no gaps in it.
items.why: Succession diagrams are drawn as a straight line ending at 'climax', and the climax is described as stable, which students read as unchanging. The guide requires students to appreciate that in some ecosystems there is a cycle of communities. Old heather plants die back, opening gaps colonized by lichens and mosses before heather seedlings re-establish; the ecosystem persists, but through a cycle rather than a fixed end state.
items.specStatementText: Some ecosystems cycle instead of settling
items.random_wrong: The repeated dying back of the heather shows that the ecosystem is unstable and is degrading towards collapse.

items.q: Sheep have grazed a hillside for centuries and it is covered by grassland. When grazing was stopped on a fenced plot, shrubs appeared within ten years and young trees within twenty. What does this show?
items.correct: Grazing had arrested succession, holding the hillside at a grassland stage below its climax community.
items.misconception: Grassland is the natural climax community here, and fencing disturbed it and began a new succession.
items.why: Students equate persistence with climax and do not distinguish a community maintained by a human influence from one maintained by the environment alone. The climax community is the one that succession tends to lead to under the given environmental conditions. Grazing by farm livestock is an example of a human influence that prevents the climax from developing; when grazing stops, scrub and then trees appear.
items.specStatementText: Climax communities and how humans arrest succession
items.random_wrong: The shrubs and trees must have been planted, because succession cannot resume once it has been arrested by human activity.

items.q: How does drainage of a wetland for agriculture affect ecological succession there?
items.correct: It prevents the community that the wet conditions would naturally lead to from developing, so the land stays as farmland.
items.misconception: The wetland community cannot re-establish afterwards, because succession stops permanently once the wetland has been drained.
items.why: Human impacts are presented as permanent damage, and students assume that a community that has been held back has lost its capacity to change. Arrested succession is maintained only while the influence continues. Fenced plots on grazed hillsides develop scrub and trees within decades of grazing ending, and rewetted wetlands regain wetland communities, showing that the natural processes of succession are still available.
items.specStatementText: Climax communities and how humans arrest succession
items.random_wrong: The drained farmland is now the climax community for the new, drier conditions, so no further succession is possible there.

items.q: A farm sprays insecticide and herbicide several times each season. Downstream, insect and amphibian numbers have fallen and residues of the sprays are found in well water. Which factor affecting the sustainability of agriculture do these observations illustrate?
items.correct: Pollution due to agrochemicals, since the sprays have harmed non-target organisms and contaminated water beyond the farm.
items.misconception: Leaching of nutrients, since sprays act only on pests within the field, so the downstream losses must be due to fertilizer.
items.why: Pesticides are named by their target ('insecticide', 'herbicide') and are introduced as tools for protecting a crop, so students assume their action is specific to the pest and confined to the field. Pollution due to agrochemicals is one of the factors affecting the sustainability of agriculture. Most pesticides are toxic to a wide range of organisms, and spray drift, run-off and leaching carry them into surrounding habitats and water, where they harm non-target species and can contaminate drinking water.
items.specStatementText: What makes farming unsustainable
items.random_wrong: Supply of inputs, since the sprays are inputs that protect the crop yield and so make the farm more sustainable.

items.q: Does a stable ecosystem show no change at all?
items.correct: No. In a stable ecosystem the overall structure and type of community persist over long periods, while population sizes fluctuate and individuals are continually replaced.
items.misconception: A stable ecosystem is one in which nothing changes: population sizes stay constant and any measured change shows that the ecosystem is not stable.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'stable' is 'unchanging', and population graphs in earlier courses often show a flat line at the carrying capacity, so students expect zero variation. Stability is a property of the ecosystem as a whole. Populations within it rise and fall, but the same kind of community persists; some ecosystems have persisted in this way for millions of years while their populations fluctuated continually.
items.specStatementText: Ecosystems can stay the same kind of place for millions of years
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must climatic variables stay constant for an ecosystem to be stable?
items.correct: No. Climatic variables can fluctuate, provided they remain within the tolerance levels of the organisms in the ecosystem.
items.misconception: For an ecosystem to remain stable, the climate must not change at all; any variation in temperature or rainfall destabilizes the ecosystem.
items.why: Students carry over the idea that 'stable' means 'constant', and headlines about climate change and ecosystem damage suggest that any climatic change is harmful. The requirement is that climatic variables remain within tolerance levels. Temperature and rainfall vary from year to year in every ecosystem; instability results only when a variable moves outside the range that the species present can tolerate.
items.specStatementText: What an ecosystem needs to stay stable
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does rainfall fall in proportion to the area of forest that is cleared?
items.correct: Not necessarily. Moisture recycling may be maintained until a threshold area is lost, beyond which it fails and the remaining forest changes rapidly; this is a possible tipping point.
items.misconception: The effect of deforestation is proportional: clearing 10% of the forest reduces rainfall by about 10%, and there is no threshold at which the system changes suddenly.
items.why: Most relationships met in school science are linear, so students expect the effect of a change to be in proportion to its size. A tipping point is a threshold beyond which a small further change causes a large and possibly irreversible change of state. The concern for the Amazon is that beyond a certain loss of forest area, moisture recycling can no longer sustain the remaining forest.
items.specStatementText: The Amazon: a possible tipping point
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If 83% of the original forest remains, what is the percentage change in area?
items.correct: −17%. The percentage change is the loss expressed as a percentage of the original area, not the percentage that remains.
items.misconception: The percentage of the original area that remains is the same thing as the percentage change.
items.why: Both figures are percentages of the original area, and the remaining fraction is the number that is most easily calculated, so students report it as the answer to a change question. Percentage change measures the difference between new and original values relative to the original. If 83% remains, the change is 83% − 100% = −17%, a decrease of 17%.
items.specStatementText: The Amazon: a possible tipping point
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the fraction (change ÷ original value) converted into a percentage change?
items.correct: By multiplying by 100: a fraction of −0.17 is a percentage change of −17%.
items.misconception: The fraction obtained by dividing the change by the original value is already the percentage, or needs shifting by a different power of ten.
items.why: Students handle the division correctly but misplace the decimal point when converting to a percentage, or forget the multiplication by 100 altogether. Percentage change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100. A fraction of −0.17 corresponds to −17%, not to −1.7% or −0.17%.
items.specStatementText: The Amazon: a possible tipping point
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Will the organisms in a sealed mesocosm run out of oxygen?
items.correct: Not if the mesocosm is balanced: oxygen released by photosynthesis in producers is used in respiration by all the organisms, and the carbon dioxide they release is used in photosynthesis, so the gases are recycled.
items.misconception: A sealed mesocosm cannot work because the organisms will use up all the oxygen; oxygen has to be supplied from outside for anything to survive.
items.why: Students think of oxygen as something that is used up, like fuel, and do not connect the oxygen released by photosynthesis with the oxygen consumed by respiration. In a sealed mesocosm matter, including oxygen and carbon dioxide, is recycled between photosynthesis and respiration. A mesocosm fails when the balance between producers and consumers is wrong, not because sealing itself removes the oxygen supply.
items.specStatementText: Mesocosms as models of stability
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do results from a mesocosm apply directly to the natural ecosystem it models?
items.correct: Not directly. A mesocosm is a simplified model; its results suggest how variables may affect stability, but the natural ecosystem is larger and more complex, so conclusions must be applied with caution.
items.misconception: A mesocosm reproduces the natural ecosystem exactly, so whatever happens in the mesocosm is what will happen in the ecosystem.
items.why: Models are presented in school as reliable representations, and the word 'model' in everyday use suggests an accurate copy. A mesocosm is a model used to investigate the effect of variables on stability. Like all models it simplifies: it is small, contains few species and excludes many processes, so results indicate possibilities and mechanisms rather than exact predictions.
items.specStatementText: Mesocosms as models of stability
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does removing a keystone predator affect only the species it eats?
items.correct: No. Its removal changes the abundance of its prey, which in turn changes the species the prey eat or compete with, so effects cascade through the community and can cause collapse.
items.misconception: Removing a predator affects only its direct prey, whose numbers increase; the rest of the community is unaffected.
items.why: Food chains are taught as straight lines, and students trace an effect only one step along the chain rather than through the food web. Keystone species have a disproportionate impact on community structure because effects of their removal cascade through the food web. When sea otters were removed, sea urchins multiplied, kelp was grazed away, and the fish, seals and seabirds that depended on kelp forest disappeared.
items.specStatementText: Keystone species hold the community together

items.q: Is the rate of replacement of a harvested population fixed, whatever the size of the remaining stock?
items.correct: No. Replacement depends on the number of individuals left to grow and reproduce, so heavy harvesting that removes breeding adults or seeds reduces the rate of replacement.
items.misconception: The reproductive rate is a fixed property of the species, so the rate of replacement is the same however much is harvested.
items.why: Students learn reproductive rates as species characteristics and do not connect the total number of offspring with the number of parents or seeds left after harvesting. The rate of replacement is the number of new individuals or the biomass added per year, which depends on how many breeding individuals or seeds remain. Over-harvesting reduces replacement, so the sustainable harvest falls as the stock is depleted.
items.specStatementText: Is the harvest sustainable?
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When calculating the rate of replacement of a fish stock, should natural mortality be taken into account?
items.correct: Yes. Replacement is the net addition to the stock: growth and recruitment minus natural mortality.
items.misconception: The rate of replacement is the total added by growth and reproduction; deaths from natural causes do not need to be subtracted.
items.why: Students focus on the additions to a population, and natural deaths are easy to overlook because they are not observed directly. The catch must stay below the net rate of replacement. If growth and recruitment add 15% of the biomass each year and natural mortality removes 5%, the net replacement is 10% of the biomass, and a catch above this depletes the stock.

items.q: Is soil a permanent resource that regenerates as fast as it is lost?
items.correct: No. Soil forms extremely slowly, so soil lost by erosion is not replaced within a human timescale; erosion permanently reduces the capacity of land to support crops.
items.misconception: Soil is always there and forms quickly, so erosion is only a temporary inconvenience for a farm.
items.why: Soil is everywhere underfoot and appears unchanging, and students do not see the slow processes of weathering and organic matter accumulation that form it. Soil erosion is listed first among the factors affecting sustainability of agriculture because topsoil takes centuries to form and can be lost in a few seasons of ploughing, overgrazing or heavy rain on bare ground.
items.specStatementText: What makes farming unsustainable
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What contributes to the carbon footprint of a farm?
items.correct: Fuel used by machinery, but also the energy used to manufacture fertilizers and other inputs, methane from livestock, nitrous oxide from fertilized soil and carbon dioxide from land clearance.
items.misconception: The carbon footprint of farming is just the fossil fuel burned by tractors and other machinery.
items.why: Students associate carbon emissions with burning fuel, which is visible, and are unaware that the manufacture of nitrogen fertilizer consumes large amounts of energy or that livestock release methane. Carbon footprint is one of the factors in the sustainability of agriculture and includes indirect emissions. Manufactured nitrogen fertilizer is made using natural gas, so switching from manure to manufactured fertilizer increases rather than removes the carbon footprint.

items.q: Does a high BOD mean the water contains a lot of oxygen?
items.correct: No. BOD is the amount of oxygen that aerobic microorganisms will consume while decomposing the organic matter in the water; a high BOD means oxygen is being removed rapidly, so dissolved oxygen is likely to be low.
items.misconception: Biochemical oxygen demand is a measure of how much oxygen the water contains, so high BOD means oxygen-rich water.
items.why: The name contains 'oxygen', and 'demand' is misread as 'amount'; students also confuse BOD with dissolved oxygen concentration, which is measured in the same units. BOD measures the demand for oxygen created by decomposable organic matter. Eutrophication increases BOD because dead algae provide organic matter for aerobic bacteria; the resulting consumption of oxygen is what lowers the dissolved oxygen concentration.
items.specStatementText: Eutrophication and biochemical oxygen demand
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do fish die in a eutrophic lake?
items.correct: Because decomposition of dead algae by aerobic bacteria depletes the dissolved oxygen, so the fish cannot respire.
items.misconception: Fish die in a eutrophic lake because the death of plants and algae leaves them with nothing to eat.
items.why: Food chains are the main tool students have for reasoning about ecosystems, so the loss of producers is read as a loss of food rather than as a source of decomposing matter. Fish in a eutrophic lake die of oxygen depletion, not starvation. Dead algae are food for saprotrophic bacteria, whose aerobic respiration uses up the dissolved oxygen; the fish suffocate, often in large numbers in a short time.
items.specStatementText: Eutrophication and biochemical oxygen demand
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do consumers at high trophic levels take in toxins such as DDT and mercury?
items.correct: Mainly in their food: each consumer ingests the toxin already concentrated in the tissues of its prey.
items.misconception: Organisms take up pollutants directly from the water or air around them, so the concentration in an organism reflects its exposure to the environment rather than what it eats.
items.why: Pollution is pictured as something in the water or air that organisms are exposed to, and the route through food is not visible. Producers and small consumers take up the toxin from the environment, but the large concentrations in top consumers come from their food. The concentration of DDT in fish-eating birds can be hundreds of thousands of times that in the water they live beside.
items.specStatementText: Biomagnification: DDT and mercury
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are microplastics harmless to marine animals because they are so small?
items.correct: No. Microplastics are ingested by filter feeders and other animals, can block or damage the gut, reduce feeding and growth, carry adsorbed pollutants, and pass along food chains.
items.misconception: Only large pieces of plastic harm marine life; particles too small to choke or entangle an animal cannot do any damage.
items.why: The images that shape students' ideas are of turtles with bags and seals in nets, so harm is equated with visible entanglement or blockage. The guide covers both microplastic and macroplastic pollution. Microplastics are taken in by zooplankton, shellfish and fish, accumulate in their tissues and are passed to consumers, with effects on feeding, growth and reproduction.
items.specStatementText: Plastics persist, and public understanding drove action
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do microplastics in the ocean come from?
items.correct: Both from manufactured particles such as fibres and microbeads and from the fragmentation of macroplastics such as bags, bottles and nets.
items.misconception: Microplastics enter the sea only as manufactured particles such as microbeads; larger items of plastic are a separate problem.
items.why: Microbeads were the focus of publicity and bans, so students associate microplastics only with that source. Because plastics are non-biodegradable, every macroplastic item in the sea is a future source of microplastics as it fragments; reducing macroplastic pollution is therefore also a way of reducing microplastic pollution.
items.specStatementText: Plastics persist, and public understanding drove action
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is publishing research findings in a scientific journal enough to change what citizens do?
items.correct: No. Scientists can influence the actions of citizens if they provide clear information about their findings; wide public communication, including through popular media, is what changed perception of plastic pollution.
items.misconception: Once scientific findings are published, public behaviour and policy change automatically; media coverage adds nothing scientific.
items.why: Students see science as producing facts and assume facts speak for themselves, without considering how findings reach the public. The NOS point in this statement is that scientists can influence citizens when they communicate their findings clearly. Popular media coverage of the effects of plastic on marine life changed public perception globally and drove measures such as bans on microbeads and single-use bags.
items.specStatementText: Plastics persist, and public understanding drove action
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Were measures against plastic pollution driven by public emotion rather than science?
items.correct: No. The public response was to clearly communicated scientific findings about the effects of plastics on marine life; the media coverage conveyed the research, and the resulting measures addressed a problem the research had documented.
items.misconception: Bans on plastics were an emotional reaction to television images and had no scientific basis.
items.why: Students contrast 'science' with 'emotion' and 'the media', and assume anything that spread through popular media cannot count as a scientific influence. The images shown in the media illustrated documented research on ingestion and entanglement. Clear communication of findings is a legitimate way in which scientists influence citizens, and the resulting public perception drove action on a real problem.
items.specStatementText: Plastics persist, and public understanding drove action
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must invasive plants be removed before native vegetation can recover?
items.correct: Not necessarily. At Hinewai Reserve the invasive shrub gorse was left in place and acted as a nurse canopy, sheltering native tree seedlings that then grew through and shaded out the gorse.
items.misconception: Introduced invasive plants such as gorse must always be cleared before native forest can be allowed to return.
items.why: Students learn that invasive species are harmful and generalize this to the rule that they must be eliminated, without considering their role in succession. Gorse is shade-intolerant, so once native trees grow up through it and form a canopy, the gorse dies out. Using it as a nurse crop is the basis of the minimal-interference approach at Hinewai, and shows that ecological management need not mean removing every introduced species.
items.specStatementText: Rewilding: let natural processes do the work
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are several small, isolated reserves as effective as one connected area of the same total size?
items.correct: No. Isolated fragments hold small populations that cannot exchange individuals or alleles and cannot support wide-ranging species; re-establishing connectivity over large areas is a method of rewilding.
items.misconception: As long as the total area protected is the same, it does not matter whether the habitat is in one connected block or in many separate fragments.
items.why: Area is the measure students are given for the size of a reserve, and the needs of animals to move, migrate and find mates are not obvious. Rewilding includes re-establishing connectivity of habitats over large areas. Connected habitats allow animals to move between areas, maintain larger and more genetically diverse populations, and support apex predators that need large ranges.
items.specStatementText: Rewilding: let natural processes do the work
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do pioneer species change the environment in order to make way for later species?
items.correct: No. Pioneer species change the soil and microclimate as a side effect of living and dying; these changes happen to favour other species, which then outcompete the pioneers. There is no purpose in the process.
items.misconception: Pioneer species prepare the ground so that the next species can move in; succession proceeds towards its goal of a climax community.
items.why: Succession is often described in narrative form ('pioneers pave the way'), and students assume that a sequence with a predictable end must be directed towards that end. Succession is the outcome of competition and of environmental change caused by organisms, not of any intention. Nitrogen-fixing pioneers enrich the soil because that is a consequence of their biology; the enrichment then allows competitors to replace them.
items.specStatementText: Succession and what triggers it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is succession that takes place on soil formed by earlier stages secondary succession?
items.correct: No. Primary succession includes all the stages that follow the colonization of bare rock or sand where no soil existed; secondary succession begins where a previous community has been removed but its soil remains.
items.misconception: Any succession taking place on soil is secondary succession, so only the very first lichens on bare rock are part of primary succession.
items.why: The distinction is taught as 'primary = no soil, secondary = soil present', and students apply it to each stage rather than to the starting point of the whole sequence. The type of succession is defined by how it starts. Succession on ground exposed by a retreating glacier is primary throughout, including the stages when soil has formed; succession on abandoned farmland or after a fire is secondary because soil and seeds remain.
items.specStatementText: Succession and what triggers it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does primary production fall as the plants of a succession become large, slow-growing trees?
items.correct: No. Primary production increases during primary succession, because the total photosynthesising leaf area and the depth of soil and nutrients available increase, even though each large tree grows slowly relative to its size.
items.misconception: Primary production is highest in the pioneer stage and falls as slow-growing trees take over.
items.why: Students confuse the growth rate of an individual plant with the total amount of biomass produced by the whole community per unit area. The guide lists an increase in the amount of primary production as a change during primary succession. A forest has a far greater mass of photosynthetic tissue per square metre than a pioneer community of lichens and mosses, so it produces far more biomass each year.
items.specStatementText: What changes as primary succession proceeds
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must soil be present before primary succession can begin?
items.correct: No. Primary succession begins on bare rock, sand or ash where no soil exists; pioneer organisms such as lichens and mosses form the first soil by weathering rock and adding organic matter.
items.misconception: Plants can only grow in soil, so succession starts when seeds land in soil that is already present.
items.why: Every plant students have grown was in soil, and the formation of soil by organisms is not part of earlier courses. The formation of soil is one of the changes that occurs during primary succession, driven by pioneer species. This is why the earliest stages have small plants and low primary production: soil depth, water retention and nutrient content are all initially very low.
items.specStatementText: What changes as primary succession proceeds
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does cyclical change in a community show that the ecosystem is unstable?
items.correct: No. Cyclical succession is a regular pattern within a persistent ecosystem; the cycle itself is the stable state.
items.misconception: If the community keeps changing in a cycle, the ecosystem must be unstable and heading for collapse.
items.why: Stability is read as absence of change, so repeated change is interpreted as a failure of stability. Ecosystem stability means persistence of the ecosystem, which can include a regular cycle of communities. Heather moorland has persisted for centuries through repeated pioneer, building, mature and degenerate phases; the die-back of old plants is part of the pattern, not a sign of collapse.
items.specStatementText: Some ecosystems cycle instead of settling
